paragraphs.tag: This paragraph narrows the section's opening claim by unpacking the components that make up the concept being discussed, then grounds the resulting complexity with a concrete illustrative example that exposes an open question left unanswered by existing high-level guidance, thereby motivating the need for the more detailed treatment that follows.
paragraphs.text: Aspects of Writing Norms. Writing norms are comprised of many aspects, including the language, content, organization of information, and scope of the written document. Although academic venues may provide a high-level overview of the expected content and style of writing such as encouraging authors to write "clearly and concisely, avoid jargon, organize the submission to flow logically and smoothly, provide the right level of detail", it can be challenging for novice writers to apply these suggestions in their own writing, e.g., What is the expected level of detail for that audience?

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph transitions from characterizing the problem (implicit norms and the difficulty of learning them) to situating the paper's approach within a specific theoretical tradition, citing prior research that offers a pedagogical framework and signaling which strategies from that framework the current work will adopt going forward.
paragraphs.text: Learning about a Community's Writing Norms. To support writing in an academic context, prior research has proposed the cognitive apprenticeship theoretic approach to teach novices complex cognitive tasks by mimicking experienced members of the community [8]. Drawing from these ideas, our work instantiates two strategies of cognitive apprenticeship, namely modeling and reflection.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph opens the subsection by surveying a category of prior approaches, noting a common limitation associated with that category, and briefly pointing to an adjacent line of related work, thereby setting up the contrast that the subsection will develop in subsequent paragraphs.
paragraphs.text: Writing with Retrieved or Generated Additional Text. Many writing support tools facilitate writing by suggesting content that users did not write themselves. Sentence completions are a frequent form of writing assistance [2, 28]. However, direct content generation can have negative impacts such as diminishing the author's self-expression and ownership over the final text outcome [30]. Related work has also looked into providing writing inspirations [6, 14, 43].

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph situates the current work within the preceding line of research by naming closely related prior systems, then articulates a key point of differentiation—specifically the magnitude and subsequent algorithmic processing of the retrieved material—using one of those prior systems as a direct contrastive example to clarify how the present approach diverges in scale and method.
paragraphs.text: We build on this line of research by surfacing prior text as the user writes new text (e.g., Naeem et al. [37] and IntroAssist [18]). A critical difference is the much larger scale of prior text surfaced to the user and post-processed for emergent patterns in our work. For example, IntroAssist [18] presents expert-curated email examples to help users draft their help-seeking message in a professional context, while our approach uses computational methods to show many examples drawn from a large text corpus of previously published papers.

paragraphs.tag: It narrows the related-work discussion by introducing a specific prior tool that exemplifies the broader category just described, summarizing its approach and scaffolding mechanism, then uses it as a direct point of contrast to clarify how the current work's approach differs in method and scale.
paragraphs.text: Writing with Text from a Corpus. Hui and Sprouse [19] proposed a writing support tool to help college students write in a professional context assisted by scaffolded annotations. The authors proposed a checklist with multiple annotations that provide cues about the content to include in the professional email. This checklist is complemented with model texts where sections of that text have been annotated with the elements of the checklist. This approach helps users understand the overall structure and expected content while also demonstrating concrete instantiations of the high-level guidelines. Our concepts help users plan the structure and content of their writing by showing many concrete examples of how other members of their target community have written similar texts.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph surveys existing tools and approaches for discovering related examples, establishing what gap in current practice motivates and differentiates the paper's own approach to retrieval-for-writing-support.
paragraphs.text: As previously described, writers learn from inspecting examples, but finding related work with the purpose of writing support is challenging. Search engines such as Google Scholar, the ACM Digital Library, Mendeley, and Semantic Scholar typically surface documents based on topical similarity while writers need specific analogous snippets of text from the manuscript to inform their writing. Current tools also help researchers understand how their own work relates to other work [29] by contextualizing embedded citations [5], drawing connections to follow-on work directly in the paper document [40], and making recommendations based on a paper's metadata such as citations and authorship [7, 23, 39, 42] or its semantic similarity [3, 17, 23]. In contrast, our design focuses on finding related work for the purpose of writing support, i.e., that helps writers identify existing writing conventions from a specific community.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph characterizes a gap in the existing body of related tools by describing the typical workflow and its drawbacks, then positions the paper's own approach as resolving that gap, thereby motivating the design choices presented in the following section.
paragraphs.text: Most interactive research tools either support analyzing related work [26, 29, 33, 38] or writing with computational help [9, 28]. In existing contexts, writers often need to navigate away from their writing environment to search for related work, scroll through the target document, select and process relevant text structures and draw conclusions about the implicit writing conventions encoded in the target document. Performing all of these steps leads to abrupt context switches and breaks the writing flow. Our approach proposes an integrated environment to support writing and searching for model text in the same interface, thereby minimizing the number of context switches and streamlining the writing and research process.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph opens the section by stating the overarching purpose and core design approach of the system being introduced, framing the detailed subsections that follow.
paragraphs.text: We designed CorpusStudio to support writers in learning about and applying community-specific writing norms. This is achieved primarily through novel mechanisms for the retrieval and rendering of content from a corpus of existing documents written by and for that community.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph states the section's core design objective and an accompanying constraint, framing the overarching aim and a boundary condition that subsequent design decisions in the section must satisfy.
paragraphs.text: Our overarching design goal is to empower users with evidence of community-specific emergent norms and outliers at the document and sentence level as they write their own document for the same audience. In the process of fulfilling this overarching goal, our goal is to reduce, not facilitate, unintentional human- or AI-generated plagiarism.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph opens an illustrative usage scenario by introducing a representative persona and their situational context and goal, setting the stage for the walkthrough of system interactions that follows in subsequent paragraphs.
paragraphs.text: Alice has been working on a new interactive writing support system and is drafting her manuscript for submission to an HCI venue. She has some prior experience writing academic papers but is unfamiliar with writing papers with a focus on a system contribution. She opens CorpusStudio to learn more about her target venue's writing expectations while working on her draft.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph continues the walkthrough by showing the persona engaging with the first of the two highlighted features, illustrating through a concrete sequence of actions and decisions how the interface element is explored, interpreted, and ultimately acted upon in forming part of the user's output.
paragraphs.text: Inspecting the section titles. She looks at the ordered distribution over section titles. As shown in Figure 1A, she expands the cluster named Implementation, which typically comes after System Design and around the same location as Methods (when those sections exist in a given paper). In the expanded cluster, she observes how other authors have phrased this typical section's title, i.e., more commonly Implementation and less commonly Implementation Details or Implementation of <System Name>. Although she likes the idea of adding a system name to the title, she decides to stick with the more generic commonly chosen option for now, and finishes her paper outline of section titles in the text editor beside it.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph continues the illustrative walkthrough by depicting the persona taking the next concrete action in the scenario, showing how she interacts with a second core feature of the tool and what she learns from that interaction, thereby advancing the narrative example one step further before the following paragraph introduces how she records her resulting insight.
paragraphs.text: Inspecting the retrieved sentences. In the text editor, she starts drafting the implementation section immediately under the Implementation section title, but she does not know how she should introduce it. She writes a few words and, without moving the cursor, hits the TAB key to retrieve related sentences from other work to get a sense of what (and how) other people wrote the beginnings of their implementation sections. She notices that many authors start with "We implemented <name of the system> to do/test <some hypothesis>" while some also state their design rationale.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph extends the walkthrough by showing the persona capturing a personal takeaway from the preceding example, illustrating how the tool supports reflection and retention of insights beyond the immediate task.
paragraphs.text: Developing a personal style sheet. She bookmarks one of the retrieved sentences to remind herself of this observation and adds the note: "The first paragraph of the implementation is often formulaic and with this recognizable structure." She concludes that it is probably well accepted in the community if she starts her paragraph in a similar way.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph closes out the illustrative walkthrough by briefly indicating how the user continues to engage with the tool's capabilities repeatedly over the course of the broader task, signaling the ongoing, iterative nature of the interaction rather than introducing any new capability.
paragraphs.text: Continuing Writing. Alice continues to write down her ideas in the text editor and occasionally retrieves example sentences given where her cursor is when she needs inspiration or wants to confirm how other authors have written their manuscripts.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph serves as a transitional framing statement that restates the section's overarching purpose and introduces the theoretical lens that will guide the detailed feature descriptions to follow, setting up the reader's expectations for how subsequent subsections should be interpreted.
paragraphs.text: In this work, the evidence of community-specific emergent norms and outliers at both the document and sentence level is provided to writers in the form of extracted examples from a corpus of documents written for and by their intended audience. To facilitate the writer's recognition of these emergent norms from examples without facilitating the writer's anchoring on any one example too much, we look to theories of human concept learning:

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph introduces a theoretical concept from existing learning literature and explains the problem it addresses, using it to justify a key design rationale (showing many examples rather than few) that the system aims to embody.
paragraphs.text: Variation Theory. Regardless of whether a human or a machine is learning from examples, any learning process can fall victim to overfitting, i.e., learn a rule that does not generalize to the rest of the corpus, when trained on too little data. For example, the Variation Theory of Learning [32] was explicitly designed to minimize human overfitting when learning from examples. With only a few examples or suggestions, previous systems may cause users to anchor [46] on just one of them. By instead showing many examples, we hope the user may be (1) less likely to anchor to one of the retrieved examples (or even unintentionally plagiarize from it) and (2) more likely to observe community writing norms and possibilities without overfitting to the retrieved examples.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph introduces a second theoretical framework, complementing the one presented in the prior paragraph, to justify a specific design choice made in rendering the retrieved examples, linking that design decision to established cognitive theory about pattern perception.
paragraphs.text: Structural Alignment Theory. While the many retrieved examples in our work are not algorithmically selected on the basis of Variation Theory, the textual examples are ordered and rendered with visual attributes (e.g., grayed-out repeated words or color-coordinated highlights) designed to support the recognition of emergent commonalities and outliers, based on the human cognitive processes of pattern recognition described by Structural Alignment Theory [13].

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph transitions from the preceding theoretical grounding to a concrete description of the system by introducing the core interface component where users interact, establishing a baseline element before subsequent paragraphs elaborate on its specific capabilities.
paragraphs.text: Text Editor. Users outline their paper and draft their prose in the central text editor (Figure 1B). The editor supports two text cell types: section title and paragraph.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph shifts from the preceding theoretical framing to a concrete technical description of a core interface component, introducing it as a foundational structural element before subsequent paragraphs detail its specific behaviors and supported input types.
paragraphs.text: Borrowing from the syntax of Markdown editors, the editor allows users to create section titles by pre-pending text with #'s where the number of #'s indicate the level of the section title.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph introduces one of the two main feature categories promised earlier in the section, explaining the underlying rationale (helping users understand common and uncommon patterns at this level) and identifying the computational method used to generate the visualized output, thereby transitioning from the general theoretical framing to a concrete description of a specific design element.
paragraphs.text: Surfacing Document-level Community-specific Emergent Norms and Outliers. Inspecting outlines from other papers in the target community can help writers develop their own. To help writers understand how papers are commonly (and uncommonly) structured within their target community at the document level, we show an ordered distribution of section title clusters from the entire corpus immediately to the left of the central text editor (Figure 1A Section Titles From Other Papers). This ordered distribution is computed by applying Positional Diction Clustering (PDC) [15] to the ordered lists of top-level section titles extracted from each paper in the corpus.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph explains the theoretical mechanism underlying a previously introduced algorithmic technique, describing how it operationalizes a cited conceptual framework and then grounding that explanation with a concrete illustrative example drawn from the system's output to show readers how the technique's results should be interpreted.
paragraphs.text: PDC is a structural mapping engine [11] designed to algorithmically emulate at scale the analogical matching process humans do when comparing two or more structurally similar objects, as described by Structural Alignment Theory [13]. In CorpusStudio, the objects are papers, and the resulting order of section title clusters that PDC generates preserves the section titles' approximate relative positions in their respective papers. For example, in Figure 1A, Introduction is the ubiquitous starting point and, in approximately 80% of papers, it is followed by Related Work. The user can also see outliers like the two papers that have a section titled An Interactive Walkthrough soon after.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph supplies implementation-level detail about how a previously introduced visual element is displayed and manipulated, specifying the quantitative indicators used to represent frequency and the interactive mechanism for revealing or concealing additional detail, thereby grounding the preceding conceptual description in concrete interface behavior.
paragraphs.text: Section title clusters are shown with a count and a proportionally long bar indicating the total number of section titles in that cluster found across the entire corpus. The most frequent section title in each cluster is chosen as the cluster name. Clicking on a cluster name expands (or closes) a cluster, showing (or hiding) all its members.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph elaborates on a feature introduced in the preceding paragraphs by explaining the specific cognitive-support mechanisms layered on top of it, detailing how visual and ordering cues are designed to help users perceive shared structure versus variation within grouped items.
paragraphs.text: We also provide cognitive support for perceiving the commonalities and variations within each cluster of section titles: The underlined words within each cluster name appear in every section title within it (a strict commonality), serving as information scent about the cluster contents when it is closed. Within each cluster, the PDC algorithm dictates the order of section titles to minimize diction differences between section titles in adjacent rows; words that appeared previously in the ordered list of cluster members are greyed out so that variations might be more visible. This text graying strategy is based on the interleaved view of PDC results in Gero et al. [15].

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph serves as a transitional framing statement that introduces the next major feature category being described, explaining its intended purpose and the general kind of insight it is meant to provide before the subsequent paragraphs detail the specific mechanism that implements it.
paragraphs.text: Surfacing Sentence-level Community-specific Emergent Norms and Outliers. This writing support is intended to provide insights into both established conventions and areas where variation is common at the sentence level. By retrieving and displaying many relevant sentences simultaneously, users can observe how similar content is expressed across different papers. These distributions can reveal both rigid conventions (narrow distributions) and areas of flexibility (wide distributions). For instance, participant descriptions in user studies often follow stereotypical patterns, while discussion sections typically show more variation to accommodate novel findings.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph introduces and defines a core technical mechanism underlying one of the features described in the section, explaining at a conceptual level how it combines multiple inputs to produce its output and pointing the reader to later sections for implementation specifics.
paragraphs.text: Spatial Retrieval. At the core of our approach is a novel retrieval mechanism we call analogous spatial retrieval, which integrates context, content, and spatial information. Users can request this retrieval of sentences from other papers by hitting the TAB key as they are drafting their text. Given where the user's cursor is placed in the text editor at the moment of retrieval (i.e., the text of the currently focused paragraph cell and the title of the section containing it), we retrieve and display many potentially analogous sentences from similarly titled sections of papers in the corpus (Figure 1C What others wrote column) as well as the subsequent sentence in each paper (Figure 1C What they wrote next column). See Section 3.4 and Section 4.2 for more spatial retrieval implementation details.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph extends a previously introduced mechanism by describing an additional interaction technique that builds on it, explaining how a secondary user action modifies the mechanism's behavior to serve a related but more advanced purpose.
paragraphs.text: To further help writers "peek into the future," that is, explore what other authors wrote later in a given section, users can insert empty paragraph cells after a non-empty paragraph cell and then trigger sentence retrieval. The number of empty cells corresponds to the offset o (in sentences) to be retrieved from the corpus. Retrieving content with an offset works by first retrieving all sentences that would have been retrieved if the cursor had been in the nearest preceding non-empty paragraph cell but then retrieving and displaying the o-th subsequent sentences.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph justifies a specific design parameter by connecting it to the theoretical rationale established earlier in the section, then reports an informal exploratory comparison of alternative settings that led to the chosen value, bridging conceptual motivation and concrete implementation choice.
paragraphs.text: Scale of Retrieval. Following Gentner's work on analogical learning theory [13], the comparison of many example sentences promotes the extraction of common principles or abstract schemas, which may be more likely to be transferred to future writing tasks. We experimented with displaying 10, 25 and 50 sentences at once and found that 25 sentences provided enough content for writers to explore and potentially recognize common principles and abstract schemas while not overwhelming them.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph elaborates on a previously introduced feature by explaining the underlying rationale for its design choice (linking it back to a theoretical principle cited earlier), then enumerates and contrasts the specific alternative implementations offered to the user, detailing the mechanism by which each one operates.
paragraphs.text: Sentence Rendering. However, what writers learn from these examples depends not only on their scale and variety, but also on how the writer mentally processes and compares them [13]. To aid in this mental sentence comparison process, the sentence examples can be rendered with algorithmically assigned visual variables (e.g., color-coordinated highlights) designed to support the recognition of emergent commonalities and outliers (and possibly support the mental cross-sentence alignment process necessary for developing abstract sentence schemas). Figure 2 shows a comparison of the two available but optional rendering modes: • Distinctly Colorize Recurring Words. We created a color map based on the twenty most-frequently occurring words across all retrieved sentences and columns (excluding stop-words), then iterated through each retrieved sentence and colorized the other word occurrences using the color map. This mode is the default. • Grey Out Repeated Words. This mode de-emphasizes previously seen words by iterating through each retrieved sentence and greying out words that have appeared in any of the previous sentences in the result list.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph introduces an additional interactive mechanism within the system, explaining how a user-initiated action triggers a reordering and recomputation of the previously described output, thereby extending the section's account of supported interactions beyond the initial rendering and retrieval behavior already covered.
paragraphs.text: Re-ranking is another way for users to explore relationships across sentences. When users click on the re-ranking icon (arrow below bookmark icon next to each sentence), the selected sentence moves to the top of its column in Figure 1C. CorpusStudio then sorts the other sentences in ascending cosine-distance from that new top sentence. This triggers the system to recompute the greyed-out words to account for the new sorted column.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph introduces another specific interface feature within the broader feature inventory, explaining its mechanism and purpose, and noting a supplementary capability for exporting the resulting user-generated content to support external sharing.
paragraphs.text: User Notes. As shown in Figure 3 and the top right callout in Figure 1C, users can bookmark a sentence and then comment on it in the User Notes section, e.g., with a reminder of why it fulfills its purpose particularly well or poorly. These annotated sentence examples can be exported as a csv file to facilitate sharing observations, preferences, and insights with others.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph introduces a supplementary interface feature that addresses a potential gap left by the preceding core feature description, explaining how it supplies additional contextual detail and provenance information on demand to prevent misinterpretation of the surfaced material.
paragraphs.text: Contextual Tooltips. Writers may want to know more of the context surrounding a retrieved sentence, e.g., to avoid misinterpreting it. As shown in Figure 1D, users can hover over a retrieved sentence to view a floating window showing the paper's title, the hierarchical section title path, and the sentences immediately before and after. The paper title links to the full paper in the ACM Digital Library. Additionally, if any retrieved sentence includes a citation, users can hover over it to display the full citation information, including the authors and the referenced paper title.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph articulates the underlying rationale for a preceding cluster of design decisions, explaining how the combination of features is collectively intended to achieve a stated non-functional goal rather than introducing a new feature itself.
paragraphs.text: Features for Promoting Learning, not Plagiarism. A combination of features are intended to work together to support users in actively engaging with many examples, rather than anchoring on and copying any one. More specifically, showing multiple examples at once may help novice writers make more informed decisions about plagiarism: when sentences are highly similar across papers, this often indicates accepted community writing norms (like in methodology sections), while sections with more varied writing styles suggest areas where similar phrasing should be avoided.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph extends the preceding discussion by introducing supplementary design decisions that reinforce the stated goal, clarifying how they work together with the previously described mechanism to achieve the intended outcome.
paragraphs.text: In concert with showing many examples, two additional design choices are intended to further facilitate learning over plagiarism: First, we disable the user's ability to copy and paste retrieved sentences into their own draft. Second, by providing visible affordances for saving and annotating their insights, we may promote deeper reflection on the writing patterns they observe.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph grounds the preceding conceptual description in concrete engineering terms by specifying the technology stack, infrastructure, and deployment setup used to realize the system, establishing the practical feasibility of the approach before the section moves on to discuss specific implementation choices in greater depth.
paragraphs.text: We implemented our system as a web application using SvelteKit. For sentence retrieval, we used WeaviateDB as our vector database, using its built-in text embedding capabilities and approximate k-Nearest Neighbor (kNN) search implementation [34]. The system was deployed on a workstation with 12 GB of GPU memory and made remotely accessible to study participants.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph justifies a specific technical design decision by acknowledging the underlying complexity of the general problem, citing established precedent for the chosen approach, noting an alternative that was explored, and explaining why empirical testing led to favoring the simpler method over the alternative.
paragraphs.text: While determining relevance in retrieval systems is inherently complex and depends on users' dynamic writing objectives, querying based on semantic similarity in text vector space is an established approach in retrieval-based systems [47]. Our initial implementation explored hybrid search techniques, following prior work that used Reciprocal Rank Fusion [41] to combine keyword-based and vector-based retrieval results. However, through initial experiments, we found pure vector-based search provided more contextually relevant matches.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph opens the section by establishing the provenance and scale of the dataset used, specifying the sources, time range, and total quantity of documents collected, as well as noting the administrative step taken to obtain permission to use the material, thereby grounding the subsequent methodological subsections in a concrete data foundation.
paragraphs.text: We collected 478 papers from two HCI venues (IUI and UIST) which included the proceedings from 2021 until 2023. These venues typically publish HCI system contributions. We completed the data request process with the ACM.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph justifies a methodological choice in the data preparation pipeline by recounting an initial approach that proved inadequate, explaining the alternative technique adopted instead, and noting what accompanying information was preserved during this processing step.
paragraphs.text: We initially used the NLTK module to split each manuscript into sentences, but we experienced many edge cases where extracted sentences were incomplete. We therefore chose an LLM-based approach instructing the model to separate sentences by inserting [EOS] tokens between sentences. For each extracted sentence, metadata was also saved, e.g., the context shown in the tooltips described in Section 3.3.5.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph specifies the technical procedure used to generate vector representations of the data, naming the method's inspiration, the preprocessing step applied before encoding, the specific tool and model used, and the rationale for why this approach enables the intended retrieval capability described earlier in the section.
paragraphs.text: To implement spatial retrieval, we follow an approach resembling LangSmith [20]. We prepared our corpus to support this functionality by pre-pending section titles to the extracted sentences before embedding the concatenated sequence using OpenAI's 'text-embedding-small-3' model (Figure 4). This approach enables CorpusStudio to retrieve related sentences based on both the section title and the content of the sentence. We used default parameter values and default un-trimmed vector dimensions.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph explains the methodological procedure used to derive the section's core data structure, specifying the extraction and clustering process applied and noting how an auxiliary quantitative measure was computed to support a visualization element, thereby establishing the technical basis the reader needs before encountering the resulting outputs.
paragraphs.text: The sequences of top-level section titles for each paper were extracted and organized into a list of lists using positional diction clustering (PDC) [15]. This is identical to the process that produced the data for the Interleaved PDC view in Gero et al. [15], except instead of processing LLM responses as sequences of sentences, we processed papers as sequences of section titles. We also computed how many papers had each section title in order to populate a corresponding histogram in the CorpusStudio interface.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph justifies a specific implementation parameter by reporting a brief exploratory test of alternative values, explaining why one was ultimately selected for the prototype.
paragraphs.text: We experimented with different sample sizes ranging from 200, 500, 1000, to 5000 section titles and found that distinctive distribution characteristics quickly emerged even with smaller sample sizes. For our prototype we decided to render and cluster 1000 section titles to demonstrate both the defining characteristics of the section title distribution while still providing a variety of ways authors have organized and phrased their section titles.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph opens the section by framing the overall evaluation approach, stating the study design type, outlining the tasks participants completed, clarifying terminology used with participants and the chosen baseline comparison condition, and articulating the research questions the study aims to address.
paragraphs.text: To evaluate our two novel writing support concepts (described at the document level in Section 3.3.2 and at the sentence level in Section 3.3.3), we used CorpusStudio to conduct a controlled within-subjects experiment with participants who were, with one exception, actively working towards writing a manuscript for an HCI venue. Participants completed two writing tasks during the user study: (i) drafting or revising an outline of their paper and (ii) drafting or revising section(s) of their paper. We referred to CorpusStudio as a "set of design features" or "prototype" during our user evaluation of the concepts. We used Google Docs as our baseline interface because it is a commonly used writing environment in this context. We aimed to investigate how participants would use the writing supports to achieve their goals, how the supports would affect their writing process, and how they may help them identify norms of a target community.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph establishes the study's participant sample by reporting recruitment sources and demographics, quantifying relevant prior experience levels, and presenting a standardized trait measure to characterize the sample's general disposition relevant to the task.
paragraphs.text: Sixteen participants were recruited through mailing lists and Slack channels from different universities in the USA, Germany, United Kingdom and South Korea (Table 1). Participants had most commonly authored or co-authored 3-5 academic papers already, but two had authored less and four had authored more than twenty (see Appendix Figure 12 for the entire distribution). The average Need for Cognition (NCS-6) score [31] across all participants was high—4.57 out of 5 (standard deviation: 0.46)—so participants were particularly willing to exert cognitive effort on a given task.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph supplements the participant profile by reporting additional characteristics relevant to the study context, specifically their target audience and the extent to which they consult prior published examples in their own work, situating the sample within the task domain the study addresses.
paragraphs.text: Most participants were targeting HCI venues, and one was targeting a machine learning venue. All participants reported referencing published papers during their writing process: 50% always did, 30% (5/16) often did, and 20% (3/16) sometimes did.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph rounds out the participant profile by reporting prior exposure to and frequency of use of comparable existing tools, establishing a baseline of familiarity against which the study's findings can later be contextualized.
paragraphs.text: All but one participant had previously used at least one writing support tool. Tools included Grammarly (12), DeepL (3), ChatGPT (4), Google Docs add-ons for reference search (1), Zotero plugins (1), SciSpace (1), and OpenAI’s Grammar Checker plug-in (1). Usage frequency varied: 2/16 used them occasionally, 6/16 used them a few times per month, 5/16 a few times a week, and 3/16 once a day or more.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph opens the procedural account by specifying the logistical and administrative framework of the study sessions—mode of delivery, facilitation, access requirements, duration, and participant compensation—before detailing the substantive steps participants undertook.
paragraphs.text: All studies were conducted remotely via Zoom and were evenly facilitated between the two lead co-authors. CorpusStudio was accessible as a web application, so participants were not required to install anything. Each study took approximately 60-75 minutes, and participants received $25 (USD) via digital payment (Zelle, Venmo, or PayPal) as compensation for their time.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph details a specific administrative step within the chronological walkthrough of the study procedure, describing the pre-study data collection instrument used to gather baseline information about participants before the main tasks began.
paragraphs.text: Consent & Pre-Study Survey. Each participant, after giving informed consent, completed a brief survey about their demographics, experience with scientific communication and writing for a target venue, current strategies for writing, use and experience with writing support tools, and questions relevant to the task that they would be completing. All survey questions are included in Appendix A.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph marks a transition in the procedure narrative by explaining a disclosure step taken before the main tasks began, clarifying why participants were given certain contextual information so that subsequent descriptions of their task engagement can be properly interpreted.
paragraphs.text: Task Preparation. Participants were informed that CorpusStudio's corpus, from which they would be viewing section titles and retrieved sentences, consisted of papers from two HCI venues, IUI and UIST, between 2021 and 2023. This information was disclosed to ensure participants had a clear understanding of the corpus context, allowing them to engage with the examples accordingly, regardless of their own specific target venue.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph describes a procedural safeguard applied before each task begins, explaining how participants were briefed on the relevant concept being tested and clarifying the evaluative framing (that the tool, not the participant, was under evaluation) so as to reduce performance anxiety and ensure consistent task understanding across participants.
paragraphs.text: Before starting each of the two tasks, participants watched a tutorial video that explained the relevant writing support concept and its supporting features in CorpusStudio. Participants were told that we evaluated the features, not their work.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph introduces and justifies the rationale for the first of the study's two tasks, explaining why this particular activity was chosen as a means to observe a specific aspect of participant behavior before the procedural details of that task are laid out in subsequent paragraphs.
paragraphs.text: Task 1: Outline Writing. We chose outlining as our first task because it let us examine how participants structured their work after seeing an ordered distribution over section titles from published papers.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph specifies the procedural details of the first experimental task, explaining its rationale, structure, conditions compared, time constraints, and data collection methods, thereby operationalizing how the broader study procedure addresses one of its stated research aims.
paragraphs.text: The outlining task had two sub-tasks: drafting section titles for the first and second half of the paper. Participants used either a baseline interface (Google Docs) or the exploratory interface (CorpusStudio) in counterbalanced order. With the baseline, participants relied on their typical resources. With CorpusStudio, they just used the Figure 1A Section Titles From Other Papers feature. Each sub-task had a 5-minute limit. They thought aloud while writing and completed post-task surveys (Appendix A.2, Appendix A.3).

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph details the main experimental task of the procedure, explaining its purpose, structure, time constraints, and the concurrent data-collection methods used to capture participant behavior and responses during its execution.
paragraphs.text: Task 2: Paper Writing. Participants began writing or revising sections of their manuscript for their target venue. They were given the option to bring the outline created in the previous task and any supporting text that they may have already written into this task.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph specifies the procedural details of the second experimental task, including the time allotted for the core activity, an embedded data-collection instruction tied to the study's analytic goals, a subsequent time block for review and refinement, and a reminder of the concurrent verbal protocol used throughout.
paragraphs.text: Participants were allowed to use any feature of CorpusStudio to help them write. As part of the task, participants were asked to bookmark example sentences that they would want to save and annotate in User Notes for themselves or a mentee. They were given twenty minutes to complete the writing portion and five minutes at the end to revise and update their User Notes; they also were asked to think aloud while completing this task.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph discloses a specific procedural safeguard introduced during the task to address a known risk, explaining what information and instructions were given to participants beforehand to mitigate that risk, thereby documenting methodological controls relevant to interpreting the task's validity.
paragraphs.text: Note that, in the tutorial video at the beginning of the task, we included the information about plagiarism and patterns over retrieved sentences described in Section 3.3.6. We also provided the following instruction: "When there is high diversity of sentence content and style, read many sentences before composing your thoughts to avoid mirroring any one sentence directly; this will hopefully help you avoid plagiarism and ensure your work remains authentic."

paragraphs.tag: It marks the closing step of the procedural walkthrough, indicating the final data-collection activity that brings the session to an end after the preceding task-by-task description.
paragraphs.text: Post-Tasks Survey and Interview. To conclude the task and study, participants completed a post-task survey (see Appendix A.4) followed by a brief semi-structured interview (see Appendix A.5).

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph opens the results section by describing the analytical method used to derive the findings, establishing the procedural credibility and systematic process behind the themes presented in the subsections that follow.
paragraphs.text: The two lead co-authors analyzed the user study transcripts with a Grounded Theory approach [22]. They separately collected a list of participants' behaviors, approaches, insights, and suggestions about the interface as well as responses to initial open-ended survey questions and the final semi-structured interview questions. To derive high-level themes, both co-authors jointly organized and clustered the codes through affinity diagramming. Throughout and after this process, co-authors discussed their respective codes, resolved assignment conflicts through discussions, and refined the labeling of the clusters. Once both authors agreed on the clusters, they distributed the themes evenly among the authors who individually identified further evidence for each theme in the study transcriptions. Lastly, all authors reviewed and agreed on the final result report.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph opens the section's substantive findings with a high-level overview, summarizing the overall benefits participants experienced before the subsequent subsections break those benefits down into detailed thematic categories.
paragraphs.text: Overview. Participants reported that seeing retrieved sentences and section titles helped them overcome the blank page problem and continue drafting. They also found it helpful to view multiple contextually relevant sentences from various papers on a single page within a centralized writing environment, which allowed for easier comparison of structure and patterns. They reported that this layout was more efficient and less overwhelming than traditional methods, such as having multiple papers open to compare texts.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph extends the overview by noting a general use case for the tool, briefly illustrating the kind of concrete task it supported before the section moves into more detailed, theme-by-theme findings.
paragraphs.text: Participants used the retrieved sentences and section titles to gather ideas or mimic good writing, and found the tool helpful for tasks such as drafting introductions, starting sections, describing systems, and beginning paragraphs.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph adds a qualifying note to the section's overview by presenting a case where the studied tool did not shift users' core understanding yet still delivered secondary benefits, illustrated with a brief anecdotal example, thereby tempering the preceding claims with a more nuanced, partial counterpoint before the discussion moves into detailed subthemes.
paragraphs.text: Some participants reported that their understanding of a venue's norms remained the same after utilizing the tool, but they still found value from other aspects such as terminology, phrasing, structure, and ideas. For example, a participant noted that they were inspired to think more critically about how they wrote rather than just following norms.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph opens the subsection by situating the forthcoming findings in context, summarizing participants' prior practices and baseline approaches before the intervention was introduced, thereby establishing a point of comparison for the observations that follow.
paragraphs.text: Existing Practices for Creating Section Titles. Prior to Task 1, participants described their methods for drafting outlines. Many saved a list of papers in Google Docs or a local folder, reviewed the individual works, and aligned their section titles with papers they deemed most relevant to their topic. Some participants followed section titles from their own prior work, while others consulted colleagues familiar with their target venue or reviewed papers from the venue to follow a similar structure.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph presents observed behavioral patterns of how participants engaged with and leveraged the feature under discussion, illustrating the range of distinct approaches users adopted drawn from study observations and participant quotations.
paragraphs.text: Ways of Reading and Using the Section Titles From Other Papers Feature. Some participants entered the study with an existing notion of the section titles they needed and used the distribution of section titles as a checklist to validate their choices (P1, P3). P13 found the feature useful for identifying structure, particularly for new writers. Several participants either chose a section title from the distribution and adapted it to align with their writing goals or modified their pre-existing section title based on inspiration from the distribution. P7 decided to use the feature to find top-level section titles and then create their own subsection titles.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph extends the preceding observation by cataloguing the range of anticipated future use cases that participants volunteered when asked to reflect retrospectively on the feature, thereby broadening the evidence from in-the-moment behavior to perceived long-term value, with individual contributors attributed to each use case.
paragraphs.text: Participants used section title frequency as an indicator of norm and popularity. P10 explained, "I'm less drawn to section [titles] that only have two or one [paper they show up in] because it doesn't make me feel confident that it's common."

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph broadens the discussion from immediate usage patterns to prospective value, cataloguing participants' retrospective judgments about how the feature could serve varied future writing needs and contexts, thereby demonstrating the breadth of anticipated applicability beyond the study setting.
paragraphs.text: Post-task, participants described scenarios where the feature could benefit their work. While P1 did not find it valuable for their future writing, others identified uses such as determining paper structure (P2, P3, P4, P8, P9, P10, P11, P12), outlining early drafts (P3, P4), writing about unfamiliar subject areas or methods (P5, P6), writing for a new venue (P8), having an "external" perspective (P11), learning about research (P16), preparing to break the norm in the research (P16), prototyping an outline rapidly (P13), and navigating when they have "no idea where to start" (P15).

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph shifts from describing how users applied the feature to examining what cognitive or perceptual effect the feature had on users, presenting illustrative participant testimony to substantiate the claimed benefit before the following paragraph addresses a related but distinct nuance.
paragraphs.text: User Insights on Variation, Norms, and Breaking Norms. Participants noticed variation across section titles, noting that there were different ways to describe conceptually similar sections. Differences ranged from minor, such as singular versus plural titles (e.g., "Related Work" versus "Related Works") to more significant, like adding new details to a more generic title or the existence of a more distinct title indicating a more unusual paper component. Evaluating the distribution of titles helped some participants see an unexpected range of possible titles and exposed them to new options. For example, P2 noted, "The section titles are more diverse than I thought. There are things like, you know, 'expert interviews' which I've never done... There were a few others that I found which are pretty new to me... It definitely broadens my sort of—my horizon."

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph deepens the preceding observation by presenting specific participant examples illustrating how users engaged with outlier or less common items in the distribution, showing both adoption and deliberate divergence, and closing by noting that users retained independent judgment rather than simply deferring to the displayed frequencies.
paragraphs.text: Some participants were particularly interested in seeing titles that deviated from the norm. P3 found it helpful to visualize less common titles, which appeared only once or twice, compared to more popular ones with over a hundred instances. Some participants chose to use or adapt titles from the shown distribution, while others chose to intentionally deviate from the perceived norm of the distribution. For example, P7 decided to continue with their own drafting approach, as their paper was "more on novel contribution rather than implementation," so they believed that frequently used section titles about implementation would not be useful when describing their work. Critically, we observed that participants exercised their agency despite having access to the distribution: If they did not like how a section title was phrased, even if it was frequently used, they would opt for their own desired phrasing.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph opens the subsection by presenting initial observational findings on how participants engaged with the content, introducing variation in engagement styles and pointing to a supporting figure before the subsequent paragraphs elaborate on specific themes in greater depth.
paragraphs.text: Reading and Processing Sentences. We observed that participants read and processed what they had read in two different styles: some did selective reading by skimming across sentences, while others read sentences in their entirety. Regardless of engagement style, participants identified new takeaways. For example, P2 discovered new ways of structuring sentences through analyzing examples. Some of the (sub)communities represented in the corpus were unfamiliar to P4 and P6, and they learned about the habits reflected in that text. P14 likes control over the content of her writing, and valued learning about sentence structures that could guide her own composition choices.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph introduces illustrative examples drawn from system logs to ground the preceding observation in concrete instances, then qualifies the generalizability of those instances by noting that their relevance was contingent on each participant's individual goals and context, citing varied participant preferences as supporting evidence.
paragraphs.text: Figure 5 shows two examples of system logs (not user interface screenshots) when participants retrieved sentences given a point in their draft. Note that the relevance of these retrieved results varied depending on each user's specific writing goals and context. For example, several participants valued perceived syntax and organizational structures over content (P1, P2, P12, P10). P11 and P5 looked for concise sentences while P14 sought out more detailed examples.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph inserts a brief, isolated participant observation as a transitional data point before the discussion shifts to the next thematic topic, offering a minimal illustrative anecdote rather than developing a fully elaborated point.
paragraphs.text: P10 noted similarities in the retrieved sentences and reflected on drafting certain sections of their own.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph extends the section's argument by introducing a new recurring use pattern observed among participants, illustrating it with specific anecdotal evidence from multiple participants to show how the tool's content prompted users to notice and correct a particular type of oversight in their own work.
paragraphs.text: Aligning, Understanding, and Addressing Terminology. Writing for different venues requires aligning terminology with community expectations to ensure consistency and clarity. Misunderstandings in terminology can make a paper difficult to follow or cause confusion, as P1 noted about differing definitions of terms like "LLMs" in different venues. P6 emphasized the importance of using correct terminology, especially in the analysis section, where there are expected norms to follow to avoid confusion. Participants found that they sometimes overlooked writing about important terms, as P11 realized when seeing the word "rubric" in the retrieved results, prompting him to address it in his manuscript. However, P6 cautioned that related terms might appear in different contexts, which requires careful consideration by the reader to avoid misinterpretation.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph introduces an additional, secondary use pattern that emerged from the study data, illustrating with participant-sourced examples how the tool was repurposed for a purpose beyond its primary intended function, and closes by synthesizing this observation into a broader claim about the system's dual-purpose value before transitioning to the next identified use pattern.
paragraphs.text: Finding Related Work. Many participants used the interface as a tool to find related work to cite in their manuscript (P8, P9, P10, P11, P15, P16). Sometimes they intentionally searched for sources, while other times they came across works that highlighted a necessary concept or a limitation that they had not considered, prompting them to bookmark these sentences for later reference. P10 noted that they would use the tool more in the future to retrieve similar papers to cite and P11 would use it to find papers that included arguments related to their own work. P15 noted that they used the tool primarily for finding related work, not for identifying norms of a venue. In summary, the prototype demonstrated dual utility, serving not only as a writing aid for experienced and novice writers, but also as a research tool. Participants could develop their outline and manuscripts to align with, or break, expected norms and also discover related work for citation, all within one centralized platform.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph extends the section's thematic analysis by introducing an additional use case uncovered in the qualitative data, supporting it with illustrative participant quotations to show how the tool's benefits manifested in a specific, previously undiscussed way.
paragraphs.text: Closing Content Gaps. Writers also used the tool to address content gaps in their drafts. P11 mentioned reading a sentence that helped her connect two key aspects of her work, confirming an idea she had previously considered but had not fully decided on. Another sentence prompted her to highlight a strength of her system in her manuscript. The sentences reminded participants of details they had forgotten to include, such as participant compensation (P13). P15 used the sentences to identify gaps in their writing, stating, "It's great to read what others wrote because we perform a similar process, but we did not mention that [...] in our own writing. So it would be great if we can add those."

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph presents a thematic finding from the qualitative analysis, illustrating with participant quotes and examples how the tool's outputs affected users' emotional and evaluative stance toward their own work, including a secondary, more nuanced effect that participants drew on cross-referenced contextual information to temper their interpretation of these findings.
paragraphs.text: Confidence and Perception. Participants felt more confident in their writing when they discovered that other authors had written about similar ideas or expressed them in a similar style. They also gained confidence in their related works section when they found papers in the retrieved results that aligned with their own literature review (P8, P15). Two participants, after not finding many related results for their initial text queries, perceived novelty in their writing topics and concluded that the community might not have discussed their topic yet. For example, P8 noted that his terminology appeared in other contexts but not his specific focus. P9 saw this as an opportunity to contribute novel insights. Similarly, P4 was encouraged by the lack of similar work, noting "I'm also pretty happy that apparently this is a work that might not be yet that present [in] those two communities, or in the HCI community in general. So this is not something that I find bad, but actually something that encourages me, that I'm on the right track." Note that participants were informed at the beginning of the study that the corpus included papers from two venues over three years, so some relevant work may not have been included.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph reports participant feedback on one of two alternative interface rendering options introduced earlier, explaining the perceived benefits users attributed to it and citing specific user quotes to illustrate how it supported their task performance.
paragraphs.text: Sentence Rendering Modes. We analyzed participants' perception of the cross-sentence structure mapping engine support features and how these features helped participants process the retrieved sentences. While initially overwhelming for some, participants found distinctly colorized recurring words valuable. It helped participants scan text efficiently. P7 explained, "I can just look [for the] participants in that color rather than spending my whole time reading over every block." P4 noted, "I do like the color version the most while it could be perceived as a bit overwhelming... the color does help me find the relevant words." P6 and P9 emphasized the ability to read and skim through the text faster. The feature served multiple purposes: P8 found it helpful for providing structure, while P13 used it to guide their attention to content ("I just looked at where's like the least or the lowest redundancy").

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph extends the preceding discussion of a related visual-support feature by presenting contrasting and divided user reactions to a second, complementary feature, illustrating that reception of design elements can vary even among the same participant pool.
paragraphs.text: There were more mixed comments on and less use of greying out repeated words. P8 found it counterproductive: "I can't think of a reason that I would want to have those grayed out... These were sort of the key pieces of the sentence that I was trying to match." P12 did not even notice the feature. In contrast, P4 and P3 preferred it. P3 reported that their eyes were still drawn to greyed-out words, suggesting the words' relevance mattered more than their visual appearance.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph opens the subsection by describing the general usage pattern observed for the feature under discussion, establishing an initial behavioral baseline before the subsequent paragraph details more specific or varied applications of that behavior.
paragraphs.text: Participants used bookmarking and note-taking to manage content during their writing process (P1, P4, P10, P11, P16). Initially, they bookmarked content that "caught their interest" (P10), focusing on topic relevance (P4, P8, P10, P16) and writing style (P3, P4). When reviewing these bookmarked sentences, participants would either enhance them with notes or unbookmark them if they seemed no longer sufficiently relevant.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph extends the preceding discussion by detailing the varied purposes behind the annotation behavior introduced earlier, citing specific participant examples to illustrate each purpose, and closing with a brief caveat from a dissenting participant before summarizing the overall functional significance of the combined behaviors for both personal use and sharing with others.
paragraphs.text: Participants used notes on bookmarked sentences in several ways. Some analyzed writing techniques, with P11 examining content focus and P4 studying structural elements. Notes also served as a teaching tool (P6, P8), with P6 particularly valuing sentence-specific annotations for student guidance: "If I were planning to share this with someone else I think that'd be really useful, especially to my students [...] Being able to specifically reference the part of that paper, I think is useful." However, not all participants found notes helpful—P7 preferred editing drafts directly. Overall, this dual system of bookmarks and notes supported both content curation and reflection, while potentially enabling knowledge transfer to more junior community members.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph opens the subsection by stating the overall finding—that the feature was generally useful with one noted drawback—before the subsequent paragraphs break down that finding in detail, thereby framing the structure of the evidence to follow.
paragraphs.text: Tooltips provided useful additional context (P3, P9, P13, P12), enabling participants to contextualize retrieved sentences at the paper, section, and paragraph levels. The main critique was the additional text, which required extra effort to read.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph develops the section's broader claim by zooming into one specific level of the feature being discussed, illustrating with a participant quotation how that particular aspect provided a concrete benefit.
paragraphs.text: At the paper level, the paper title offered clues about the overall topic, helping participants determine if a sentence was discussed in a similar context. For example, P9 commented that he "ended up using that tooltip quite a lot. [...] because it was quite nice to directly make a connection from the sentence to where it came from."

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph extends the section's discussion of a specific feature by presenting a concrete example of how one level of contextual detail concretely shaped a participant's reconsideration of their own structural choices, illustrating the practical impact introduced in the preceding general claims.
paragraphs.text: When looking at the section level, participants found value in reviewing the section title path. P3 observed how other authors structured the formative study, introducing "the design" and "the steps in the study" before detailing the procedure. This led her to consider splitting her own formative study into subsections and adopting a less abrupt transition to better inform the system design.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph extends the section's examination of a feature's benefits by addressing a finer-grained level of analysis, illustrating with a specific participant example how the feature resolved ambiguity encountered at that level.
paragraphs.text: At the paragraph level, participants reported that the sentences could sometimes be ambiguous when interpreted in isolation, so they read the surrounding sentences in the tooltip for clearer context. P12 used the tooltip "to see what they're talking about before and after."

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph presents a qualifying counterpoint to the preceding positive account by noting a minority of users who made less use of the feature, citing their specific reasons in order to round out the section's evidence with a more complete, balanced picture before the section concludes.
paragraphs.text: While the tooltips were helpful for many, three participants used it less frequently (P2, P7, P14). P7 commented, "It just requires a lot of time to read it all [...] so I ended up not using it as much." P2 found that "the two columns" on the right hand side (i.e., What others wrote, and What they wrote next) provided enough context without needing the tooltip. Meanwhile, P14, writing for a different venue, felt that HCI-focused contextualization was not relevant to her work.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph opens the section by introducing its organizing theme—how feature usage shifted across different phases of the task—and supports that claim with specific participant examples contrasting early-stage versus late-stage preferences.
paragraphs.text: Overall, participants found the design features useful both early in the writing process and during iterative revisions at later stages. Section title clusters were helpful for creating an initial outline. Three participants preferred to use it in early drafting because inspecting examples of other outlines helped them plan their writing for venues or contributions that they were unfamiliar with. Commenting on the integration of retrieved sentences, P1 mentioned that he would use them in the initial phase to establish terminology and sentence structure but not later, as the style, structure, and outline would already be set. Similarly, P10 preferred not to be influenced by other papers' writing styles once his initial draft was more complete. P11 added that section title clusters and retrieved sentences are most helpful early on, when there are "fewer restrictions" on content and style.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph extends the preceding discussion of early-stage feature use by presenting a complementary set of participant accounts that shows how the same tool was repurposed for revision and iteration once drafting had progressed, thereby rounding out the section's argument that utility shifts across stages of the writing process.
paragraphs.text: Once the style, terminology, and structure were set, e.g., when participants had written a complete paragraph, some participants shifted focus to refining their own writing rather than inspecting others' work—but not all. Two participants (P8, P11) mentioned that they would use section title clusters in later stages to revise their outline, either to "check the framing of the paper" or adjust subsection titles. P3 suggested using the feature in different iterations of the paper to revise sections already written, explaining that she would "highlight that section and compare it", via sentence retrieval, to similar work in the venue. Likewise, P4 noted that she would revisit the section titles, as the outline evolves during the writing process and may no longer align with the original version.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph closes the subsection by shifting from individual strategies to a broader coping mechanism users adopted when faced with the full set of tool features, using a representative participant quote to illustrate how selective engagement helped manage cognitive load, thereby offering an interpretive takeaway that synthesizes the preceding examples into a general observation about usability trade-offs.
paragraphs.text: Some participants developed strategies to manage the complexity of all the features available to them. Often, they primarily focused on the What others wrote column, consulting the What they wrote next column and contextual tooltips only when needed for deeper understanding. P2 observed: "I didn't look at the 'What they wrote next' column that much... I also didn't look at the tooltips a lot, because I don't know. I was too absorbed by the 1st column—what others wrote. And because I, at a given position or location in the paper... I was just trying to focus on what to write then." This selective attention may have helped them balance the information these features provided with the inherent cognitive load of lots of text that cognitive supports like special text rendering might not completely mitigate.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph closes the subsection by reporting the overall outcome of the design measures described earlier, confirming through observed participant behavior whether the intended safeguard against the targeted risk actually held in practice.
paragraphs.text: We implemented measures intended to promote learning and prevent plagiarism. As expected, while participants drew inspiration from the retrieved sentences, none showed an intent to plagiarize. Instead, they emphasized the importance of (i) modifying any examples to avoid plagiarism and align with their own ideas and (ii) saving work of interest to reference in their own paper, suggesting a strong awareness of the need to draft an original manuscript and cite properly.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph serves as an introductory framing statement for the section, outlining the analytical method applied to survey data and specifying which comparisons and conditions were examined across the two tasks, thereby orienting the reader to the structure of the results that follow.
paragraphs.text: We analyzed participants' responses to survey questions using a non-parametric Mann-Whitney U test. For Task 1, i.e., outline writing, we analyzed participants' responses comparing the two sub-tasks (first half of the outline vs. second half of the outline) and two interface conditions (using a regular text editor without document-level support vs. with section title rendering in CorpusStudio). For Task 2, the prose writing task, we evaluated participants' reported frequency of using CorpusStudio features and their perceived usefulness.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph opens the subsection by reporting the first statistical comparison of the two study conditions, presenting the headline significance result along with a brief interpretive gloss that links the quantitative outcome back to the qualitative observations discussed earlier in the paper, thereby establishing the overall pattern that subsequent, more granular comparisons in the subsection will refine.
paragraphs.text: Usefulness of Drafting Tools. Participants rated the usefulness of drafting their outline in a blank document (baseline) and drafting it in CorpusStudio (Figure 6). Results indicated a statistically significant preference for CorpusStudio (p = 0.003). As discussed in Section 6.1, participants valued aspects such as creating a better structure for their outline, learning how to write for a new venue or topic, and confirming their existing titles.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph reports the statistical outcome of a secondary set of comparison items within the same experimental condition, clarifying that while an overall preference result was significant, a related cluster of finer-grained evaluation questions showed no significant differences, thereby tempering and adding nuance to the preceding positive finding.
paragraphs.text: Ease of Drafting Section Title Outlines and Venue Alignment. For both conditions, participants answered a series of questions focusing on how easily they drafted section titles that were relevant to their work, aligned with the style of the target venue, adhered to norms, included all desired aspects, and identified when others had broken norms. The average responses for each condition are shown in Figure 7. A Mann-Whitney U test revealed no statistically significant differences between the interface conditions for any of these five Likert items.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph presents a statistical comparison across the two task sub-conditions (rather than across interface conditions) for the same set of survey items, reporting one significant result and interpreting it as a possible learning or strategy-transfer effect, while noting that the remaining items showed no such difference.
paragraphs.text: Differences Between Tasks. Between the sub-tasks, i.e., drafting the first half of the document compared to the second half, there was a statistically significant difference (p=0.014) in participants' responses to the question, "It was easy to create the section title structure that my target venue expects." This suggests potential learning effects as participants found it easier to create the section title structure in the second half. Participants could have adapted their writing strategies from drafting the first half to the second half. We found no significant differences in the other questions within this category (see Appendix A.3.2 for the full questions).

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph reconciles a preceding statistical analysis that found no significant effect with qualitative evidence suggesting a real but subtler benefit, tempering the null quantitative result with corroborating observational insight.
paragraphs.text: We also evaluated whether different interface conditions impacted the ease of drafting section titles and aligning them with the target venue's expectations for both the first and second halves of the outline. Although no significant differences were found, our qualitative findings suggest that participants had greater confidence in their writing when using CorpusStudio due to the availability of examples, which helped reduce uncertainty.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph reconciles a null quantitative result with the paper's qualitative findings, suggesting that the absence of statistically significant differences does not contradict the richer evidence of subjective benefit reported elsewhere, thereby tempering the preceding statistical analysis with interpretive context before the discussion moves to related survey-based observations.
paragraphs.text: Participant Perceptions of Ease and Overwhelm. Fourteen of the 16 participants (87.5%) reported that writing the section titles in CorpusStudio with Section Titles of Other Papers made the task easier (via alleviating the blank page problem and having examples at hand in a centralized writing environment), while the remaining two participants reported that writing in the baseline interface was easier.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph supplements the preceding statistical comparison by reporting descriptive, self-reported participant perceptions (framed as proportions of the sample) about which condition felt more difficult or overwhelming and why, adding interpretive nuance to the quantitative results without introducing new statistical tests.
paragraphs.text: Nine of the 16 participants (56%) concluded that writing section titles in CorpusStudio felt more overwhelming because they had to mentally process the distribution of section titles—yet most acknowledged that, despite the initial challenge, the process was useful for generating ideas. The remaining seven participants (44%) reported that completing the task in the baseline interface felt more overwhelming because they had to begin from an empty page and they felt uncertainty about how to name and structure the section titles.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph closes out the subsection's statistical reporting by addressing a specific pair of related hypotheses (identifying norms and identifying norm-breaking), presenting the quantitative null result for both, and then tempering that null result by pointing to qualitative evidence that suggests a more nuanced interpretation than the statistics alone would imply.
paragraphs.text: Identifying and Breaking Norms. We evaluated whether there was any significant difference in participants' ability to identify norms of their target venue when reading past papers (prior to the study or during the study in the baseline condition) in comparison to reviewing the distribution over section titles. The results showed no significant difference. Similarly, for identifying when it is appropriate to break norms, no significant differences were found (see Appendix A.4.3 for the full questions). However, qualitative data highlighted that with CorpusStudio, participants more frequently reflected on breaking norms intentionally, using the example distributions and their own writing to justify deviations. While these reflections did not result in significant quantitative differences, they suggest a deeper engagement with norms during the task.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph opens the subsection by introducing a standardized workload measure used to assess participants' experience during the writing task, reporting general perceptions of difficulty and effort alongside a sense of successful task completion, thereby setting a baseline context before more granular quantitative findings are presented in subsequent paragraphs.
paragraphs.text: Based on the NASA-TLX questionnaire (Figure 8), participants found the writing task mentally demanding, which balanced with their perception of how hard they had to work. They still felt successful in completing the task.
