paragraphs.tag: This paragraph reports descriptive usage-frequency data for each individual feature under evaluation, ranking them by how often participants engaged with them and briefly noting participants' stated reasons for usage patterns, while pointing to an earlier subsection for fuller qualitative explanation, thereby grounding the overall positive usefulness ratings presented next in concrete behavioral evidence.
paragraphs.text: Participants reported on how often they used each feature (Figure 9), with the counts reflecting total reported usage across all participants while completing the writing task. The retrieved sentences in the What others wrote column was most frequently used, followed by the colorizing redundant words mode of rendering sentences, which participants reported using for reasons including finding relevant aspects, remaining focused, reading faster, and skimming text (Section 6.2.6). They also frequently used the tooltips, noting that they were useful for contextualizing retrieved sentences and identifying their source (Section 6.4). Greying out repeated words was least frequently used. Some participants did not find it useful to de-emphasize words, while others did not notice the feature at all (Section 6.2.6). There was an overall positive sentiment on the usefulness of all other features (Figure 10).

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph reports survey-based results on a specific self-reported outcome related to the study's broader research question, breaking down participant responses into categories and linking them back to supporting qualitative observations noted earlier in the section.
paragraphs.text: Eight of 16 participants (50%) answered that they had a clearer sense of when it was appropriate to break the writing expectations of the target venue after interacting with CorpusStudio while four did not think that their understanding had changed and four gave a neutral response (Figure 11). From the study, we observed that at least three people commented on deviations between their prior assumptions about the structure or content and the retrieved content (Section 6.1).

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph presents an additional survey-based result that reinforces the section's overall claim, connecting it back to the qualitative findings discussed earlier to corroborate the quantitative evidence.
paragraphs.text: All but two participants found that evaluating many sentences from previous papers gave them a better understanding of the typical writing expectations of the target venue (Figure 11). This aligns with the qualitative results where participants commented positively about the usefulness of inspecting retrieved sentences, which gave them more confidence in their writing.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph serves as a brief transitional opener for the section, signaling that the findings presented earlier will now be interpreted and situated at a higher conceptual level, and previewing that the following subsections will unpack specific threads of this reflection.
paragraphs.text: Our analysis revealed several ways that writers used CorpusStudio to support their academic writing process. Here, we reflect on our design and results on conceptual and empirical levels.

paragraphs.tag: This opening paragraph of the subsection introduces the subsection's central claim by summarizing the overall finding to be elaborated, framing the more detailed discussion that follows in subsequent paragraphs.
paragraphs.text: We found that relevance of retrieved sentences was tightly coupled with users' writing intentions, as they found different uses and rationales for integrating the retrieved results into their writing process.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph extends the section's opening claim by presenting specific observed behaviors and connecting them to an established theoretical framework from the literature, using this contrast to problematize a standard assumption in the field and arrive at a more nuanced general claim that reframes the preceding point.
paragraphs.text: Users' Diverse Applications of Retrieved Sentences. While CorpusStudio uses text embeddings to capture semantic and syntactic relationships [36], our study revealed that relevance was also determined by participants' writing goals rather than semantic similarity alone. For instance, semantically similar sentences were sometimes less useful than structurally similar ones when writers sought to understand the organization of the paper.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph extends the preceding observation by elaborating on how users' goals shaped their interaction with the tool across different levels, connecting this behavior to analogous findings in related literature, and using this pattern to challenge a standard assumption in the broader field, thereby reframing the section's central claim as a more general conceptual point.
paragraphs.text: Participants sought inspiration at multiple levels of writing: from paper organization through section titles to section-level transitions and standard academic phrases. The writers shaped these results through queries using their draft text itself, similar to patterns observed in interactions with AI in writing [10]. This challenges fundamental information retrieval assumptions about query-document similarity as an (only) indicator of relevance. While it provided a useful starting point, our findings suggest that relevance of retrieved text in writing support systems is not fixed, but dynamically constructed based on writers' immediate goals.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph extends the section's argument by presenting a secondary observation about unanticipated user behaviors and interpretive pitfalls arising from the study, then draws out a design implication that recommends how future systems should proactively address these interpretive risks.
paragraphs.text: Interpreting Retrieved Results: User Behaviors and Dataset Limitations. Our study revealed how retrieved examples influenced participants' writing in unexpected ways. When participants were looking for something specific and did not find it in the retrieved results, this led to two notable behaviors: First, participants often rephrased their text to get different results, blurring the line between writing and querying. Second, some interpreted a lack of results as evidence of their work's novelty, a problematic conclusion given CorpusStudio's limited scope (two HCI venues: IUI and UIST from 2021-2023). These findings suggest that writing support systems should actively communicate their scope and limitations, for instance by suggesting broader venue searches when topic-specific queries yield no results, helping writers make informed decisions about how to interpret search results.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph opens the subsection by situating the design choice against common alternative practice in the field, then explains the rationale behind the chosen approach and the compensatory mechanism introduced to address its anticipated drawback, while acknowledging that this mitigation was only partially successful.
paragraphs.text: While many writing support systems prioritize simplicity through aggregated results, we deliberately presented many examples (N=25) to increase the variety of examples users saw. To help users process the larger scale of information, we provided sentence rendering modes that modulate visual variables of the text in a way intended to support users in recognizing cross-sentence relationships. While it provided support, it did not eliminate all the additional cognitive demands of the extra information.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph builds on the preceding setup by interpreting the study findings as justification for the design trade-off introduced earlier, arguing that the benefits observed outweigh the acknowledged cognitive costs and framing this balance as a broader consideration for similar future design efforts.
paragraphs.text: The study results suggest that showing multiple examples at once is valuable despite its cognitive demands: seeing variations in how similar ideas were expressed helped participants distinguish between rigid conventions and flexible patterns in academic writing. This suggests a trade-off between cognitive load and learning potential, a consideration for future writing support systems that aim to support learning rather than just text production.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph closes out the section by drawing a general design implication from the preceding discussion, offering a forward-looking recommendation for practitioners facing a similar design tension rather than introducing new evidence or findings.
paragraphs.text: Given that readers have different visual preferences, we provided more than one method for cognitive support. We encourage designers who wish to show multiple parallel examples to also provide alternate ways to help users visually identify patterns.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph opens the subsection by establishing a contrast between the paper's design philosophy and a prevailing alternative approach in the field, explaining the rationale behind that choice and noting a quality-assurance property that follows from it.
paragraphs.text: Our concept provides relevant text snippets to support writing but it does not use any AI-generated text, in contrast to recent trends in writing assistant systems [27]. Instead of training AI on a corpus, we surface examples from the corpus directly. In our case, these examples can be assumed to meet the community's quality standards, because they are evaluated by its members beforehand, that is, the published papers in the corpus went through peer review.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph extends the section's opening claim by articulating a broader implication of the proposed approach, arguing for an additional benefit beyond the immediate design rationale and pointing to how a supporting feature could serve that broader, community-oriented purpose.
paragraphs.text: We argue that this approach values and supports communities. For example, it might aid communities in discovering their own community-level patterns of expression and in "onboarding" new community members. Supporting this, our design includes functionality for taking one's own notes, which might later contribute to exchanges between community members about writing norms, i.e., beyond individual interactions with our system.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph extends the preceding argument by identifying a further potential benefit of the approach, then proposes a concrete direction for future investigation that would test this claim.
paragraphs.text: This approach may also make a community's past work more discoverable to its members. Our retrieval method is based on the local text in the draft, and not on other metrics, such as paper citation counts or author metrics. In this way, our concept might contribute to discovering less well known but relevant work that the writer would not have noticed otherwise. This could be examined in a dedicated future study, and the UI design could be developed further in this direction.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph situates the work's design choices within a cited theoretical framework from prior literature, drawing an analogy to a related example of embedding cognitive strategies into interface design before asserting that the current work follows a similar pattern, thereby grounding the discussion's claims in an established conceptual lineage.
paragraphs.text: Tankelevitch et al. [44] recently motivated designing for metacognitive challenges in interaction. One emerging approach here is to do so by embedding specific thinking strategies directly into the interface. For instance, Dang et al. [9] designed for the strategy of "reverse outlining" by providing a sidebar of paragraph-wise summaries, updated live. Similarly, we designed for learning from examples, with respective material provided in sidebars directly within the writing environment. Our design also supports the externalization of users' self-reflection (e.g., what does this mean for my text?) in User Notes. As our results show, participants found this helpful and made use of it in diverse ways.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph closes out the section by connecting a specific prior theoretical recommendation back to the study's observed outcomes, showing how the empirical results corroborate that external framework and thereby reinforcing the section's overall argument with a concluding, validating link between theory and evidence.
paragraphs.text: Tankelevitch et al. [44] also suggests "support[ing] users in increasing their self-awareness and adjusting their confidence." We observed that, by becoming aware of what authors in a community wrote, many participants' confidence levels increased with respect to writing for that same community.

paragraphs.tag: This paragraph closes the section by tempering the study's findings with scope caveats tied to participant and corpus characteristics and task framing, then points to unaddressed contexts and a methodological constraint (limited task duration) as directions for future investigation.
paragraphs.text: Our results reveal how writers interact with and perceive examples retrieved from a community-specific document corpus. However, readers should be cautious when generalizing these findings beyond the scope of our study. All participants had a background in HCI, and the corpus was drawn from two HCI venues, focusing primarily on system contribution papers. Additionally, the writing task was based on an academic writing scenario. Future research should explore other writing contexts where communities play a role, such as fiction, poetry, or argumentative writing. In our user study, participants were given 20-25 minutes to draft their text and engage with the various system features. While this offered valuable insights into their interactions and perceptions of the writing environment, it would be worthwhile to explore how prolonged use of these features might influence users' writing habits and style.

paragraphs.tag: As the sole paragraph of the conclusion section, it synthesizes the paper's core contribution into a closing statement, recapping the overall approach and its mechanism, contrasting it with alternative approaches to underscore its distinctive value, and ending with a broader statement of the work's intended impact and guiding principle for the field.
paragraphs.text: CorpusStudio is a writing support system that integrates example retrieval—at both the document level and sentence level—directly into the drafting process. Writers can compare their text against a curated corpus from their target academic community, with the system presenting many real examples in parallel. This tight coupling between writing and retrieval enables authors to identify established writing patterns, understand community conventions, and validate their writing choices through direct comparison with published work. Unlike systems that generate or remix text, CorpusStudio deliberately preserves and attributes original manuscripts, using search based on text embeddings that incorporate spatial information and context to surface relevant examples in an accessible format. Thereby we support academic writing while maintaining transparency and acknowledging existing scholarship. Our work aims to advance an interaction model where writing support tools help authors overcome writing barriers while respecting and learning from the contributions of others in their field.
